reflections.summary: Won game 3 and the series 2-1 because the Charizard Y/Raichu lead immediately pressured Gholdengo-Sinistcha, removed Gholdengo on turn 2, and preserved a favorable endgame. Venusaur then slept Tauros and Milotic while Dragonite supplied a protected Tailwind turn; Charizard's later re-entry overwrote Milotic's rain and enabled immediate Solar Beam pressure. The four brought—Mega Charizard Y, Raichu, Venusaur, and Dragonite—fit this opponent well: Charizard checked Gholdengo and Sinistcha, Venusaur ignored Rage Powder and controlled Tauros/Milotic, Raichu pressured Gholdengo/Milotic, and Dragonite gave speed support plus Tauros cleanup. Mega Charizard Y was the correct evolution. No evidence identifies specific between-game changes, but the game-3 selection and execution clearly helped rather than backfired. Series prep correctly prioritized the Charizard/Venusaur sun core and complementary speed/control tools. There is insufficient evidence to judge whether Kingambit, Sableye, or the four unregistered Pokémon would have improved this matchup.
reflections.adjustment: For a future series, retain the Charizard Y/Venusaur core and strongly consider the same four when Gholdengo, Sinistcha, Milotic, and Tauros are shown. Lead Charizard Y with Raichu when immediate Gholdengo pressure is valuable, but preserve Charizard around Tauros's Rock Slide and use its switch-in to deny Milotic rain. Treat Sinistcha as a target for Charizard Flying damage rather than Sleep Powder, while using Venusaur's Grass typing to attack through Rage Powder. Continue prioritizing Sleep Powder into Tauros and Milotic when safe; account for Milotic Protect before committing Encore. Do not assume unshown roster members are better without further evidence.
reflections.notebook: Opponent revealed Gholdengo Life Orb with Make It Rain, Shadow Ball, Focus Blast, and Protect; it can be pressured effectively by Mega Charizard Y and Raichu. Tauros is Jolly Expert Belt Sheer Force with Rock Slide, Close Combat, Raging Bull, and Protect; Rock Slide is the key Charizard threat, while sleep and combined Dragonite/Venusaur damage controlled it well. Milotic is Modest Leftovers Competitive with Rain Dance, Hydro Pump, Ice Beam, and Protect; it can set rain to disrupt sun, but Charizard Y can restore sun on entry. Sinistcha is Bold Heatproof Sitrus with Rage Powder, Matcha Gotcha, Strength Sap, and Protect; Venusaur ignores its Rage Powder, Sleep Powder fails because Sinistcha is Grass-type, and Flying attacks are super-effective. Sinistcha showed repeated Protect use, creating punish windows once its streak is exhausted. Whimsicott and Arcanine were not brought in game 3, so their series role remains unconfirmed. Prep conclusion: the registered Charizard Y/Venusaur/Raichu/Dragonite package was well suited to the revealed four; no supported conclusion can be made about omitted draft options.

reflections.summary: Lost because the Game 3 four and preview plan were poor into Mega Charizard-Y/Venusaur sun. Gholdengo was exposed to Raichu and Heat Wave, while Tauros and Milotic were neutralized by Sleep Powder; Milotic's Rain Dance briefly helped and Raichu was removed, but it came too late to preserve the matchup. Sinistcha's Sleep Powder immunity was correct, yet its repeated Protects only delayed an unavoidable loss. With zero recorded decision errors, the main issue was preparation and team selection rather than piloting. The registered six had useful ideas—Milotic for weather and Dragonite, Sinistcha for Sleep Powder, and Tauros for immediate pressure—but the sets lacked a dependable answer to sun, sleep, and Venusaur. No own Mega evolution was used; based on the supplied evidence, there was no suitable demonstrated Mega option, and the opponent's Charizard clearly dictated the game. There is no evidence that a specific between-game adjustment helped; the observable adjustments only produced temporary gains and ultimately backfired strategically.
reflections.adjustment: Rebuild the four around reliable sun disruption and anti-sleep pressure rather than leading Gholdengo/Sinistcha into Charizard/Raichu. Preserve Milotic until Dragonite and Venusaur are contained, and use Rain Dance proactively before Venusaur can exploit sun-boosted Solar Beam. Replace or reconsider Tauros if it cannot function while Sleep Powder is available, and test Arcanine or another omitted Pokémon in that slot only after confirming its actual set. Reconsider Gholdengo unless it has a concrete role beyond Protecting once and being removed by Thunderbolt. No supplied sets justify claiming Lopunny, Furfrou, Chimecho, or Grimmsnarl was definitely superior, but the six registered were not tailored well enough to this opponent; future preparation should explicitly test the omitted options and any available Mega Stone holder against Charizard-Y/Venusaur.
reflections.notebook: Opponent's core can be Charizard-Y plus Focus Sash Venusaur, with Raichu providing Fake Out, Lightning Rod, Electroweb, and Encore, or Dragonite providing Lum Berry, Multiscale, Protect, Tailwind, and Extreme Speed. Venusaur repeatedly uses Sleep Powder and can switch between Solar Beam in sun and Sludge Bomb; do not rely on one target remaining safe after a weather change. Rain can suppress Charizard's sun, but the opponent may restore sun immediately, so weather control must be paired with immediate pressure on Venusaur or Charizard. Sinistcha's Grass typing reliably blocks Sleep Powder and is a useful redirection option, but it is vulnerable to repeated Charizard attacks and cannot win through passive Protect cycles. Milotic's Ice Beam is a credible Dragonite answer and Rain Dance is valuable, but it must be protected from early sleep and Electric pressure. Preserve the Dragonite answer, deny Tailwind where possible, and prepare a reliable plan for Venusaur's sleep turns rather than assuming weather alone solves the matchup. Re-evaluate the six registered and every set for this sun/sleep matchup before a rematch; do not assume the omitted Pokémon are worse without testing them.
